title: The Boy Who Raced the Wind
summary: A boy who loves running imagines he is racing the wind during his coastal practice runs, and this playful game helps him push through tiredness to finish strong in his school's cross-country race.
poll: Imagining a fun game while you practice makes hard work feel easier.

versions.title: The Boy Who Raced the Wind
versions.text:
Yousef loves to run. He runs by the coast every day. This is his practice.

He likes to play a little game. He races the wind! He runs as fast as he can. The wind blows past him. He feels happy.

One day, his school has a big race. It is a long race. All the kids will run it.

During the race, Yousef feels tired. His legs feel weak. He wants to stop.

Then he thinks of his game. He races the wind again! He runs faster and faster. He feels strong.

Yousef finishes the race. He does not come first. But he tries his best. His coach is proud of him.

versions.title: The Boy Who Raced the Wind
versions.text:

He likes to play a fun game. He imagines that he is racing the wind. He pumps his arms and runs as fast as he can. The wind rushes past his face. This game makes him smile.

One day, his school has a big race. It is a long cross-country race. Every student in his class must run it.

During the race, Yousef starts to feel very tired. His legs feel heavy. He wants to stop running.

Then he remembers his fun game. He imagines racing the wind again. He runs faster and faster. Soon he feels strong again.

Yousef finishes the long race. He does not come in first place. But he tries his very best. His coach is proud of him.

versions.title: The Boy Who Raced the Wind
versions.text:
Yousef really loves running. He never misses a morning. Before school each day, he runs along the sandy coast near his home. The waves crash softly on the shore. This quiet run is his daily practice. It helps him grow stronger.

He likes to play a special game inside his head. He imagines that he is racing against the wind itself. It feels like a friendly rival is beside him. He pumps his arms and runs as fast as he can. The cool wind rushes past his face. This little game makes the hardest parts of his run feel more fun.

One day, his school announces a big cross-country race. The whole class has been waiting for it. It is a long race around the school field. Every student must take part.

Partway through the race, Yousef starts to feel very tired. His chest begins to burn. His legs feel heavy and sore. A small voice tells him to stop.

Then he remembers his special game from the coast. He imagines racing the wind once again. He pictures it rushing past him just like at home. He pushes his tired legs faster and faster. Soon he feels strong again.

Yousef finally finishes the long race with a burst of speed at the end. He does not come in first place. But he tries his very best from start to finish. His coach smiles and tells him he is proud of his hard work.

versions.title: The Boy Who Raced the Wind
versions.text:
Yousef has loved running for as long as he can remember. Every morning before school, he jogs along the sandy coast near his home. Gentle waves roll onto the shore, and a light breeze drifts in from the sea. This quiet routine is his daily practice. Over many months, it has made him stronger and quicker.

While he runs, Yousef plays a private game in his mind. He likes to imagine that he is racing against the wind itself, like a playful rival running beside him. He pumps his arms and pushes his pace faster and faster. He feels the breeze rush past his face, as if the wind were trying to keep up. This small game turns hard parts of his run into something exciting instead of tiring.

One day, his school announces a cross-country race. The whole class has been waiting for it all year. It is a long race around the school field, and every student must take part and try their best.

Partway through the real race, Yousef feels completely exhausted. His chest burns, and his legs feel impossibly heavy. A quiet voice in his head tells him to slow down or stop.

Just then, he remembers his favorite game from the coast. He closes his eyes and imagines racing the wind once more. With fresh determination, he pushes his tired legs faster and faster. Soon his strength begins to return.

Yousef crosses the finish line with one last burst of speed. He does not finish first, but he has given the race all his determination. His coach claps and tells him how proud he is of his effort and his steady pace.

Before school begins, he jogs along the sandy shoreline, where gentle waves roll steadily onto the beach and a light breeze drifts in from the open sea, carrying the faint, familiar scent of salt that he associates with calm concentration. This disciplined routine is his daily practice, and over many months it has gradually transformed him into a runner with considerably greater stamina than he once possessed, a change his classmates have begun to notice and admire.

While he runs, Yousef engages in a private mental exercise, one he has practiced since he was considerably younger, having discovered how much more enjoyable running could become through deliberate imagination. He likes to visualize himself racing against the wind itself, as though it were a playful, invisible rival jogging beside him stride for stride, matching his every movement with uncanny precision. He pumps his arms rhythmically, lengthens his stride, and accelerates his pace steadily, feeling the breeze rush past his face as if the wind itself were struggling to keep pace with him. This small act of deliberate visualization transforms even the most grueling stretches of his run into something genuinely exhilarating rather than merely exhausting, and it has become an indispensable technique he relies upon whenever running begins to feel especially arduous.

He closes his eyes and visualizes racing the wind once again, picturing the same playful breeze chasing closely behind him exactly as it does during his quiet mornings at home. Drawing on sheer perseverance, he forces his tired legs to move faster and faster, refusing to let the creeping doubt win, and before long his strength and confidence return in full force, almost as though the wind itself had lent him a portion of its energy.

He does not finish first, but he has poured every ounce of perseverance he possesses into the race from start to finish, holding absolutely nothing back for the final stretch. His coach claps enthusiastically and tells him how proud he is, not only of his effort, but also of the remarkable endurance and steady pace he maintained all the way to the finish line, a lesson in perseverance that Yousef carries with him long after the race has ended.

versions.text:
For as long as he can remember, Yousef has loved running, and scarcely a morning passes without a quiet run along the Red Sea coast near his home, a ritual that has become every bit as essential to his day as breakfast itself, woven so thoroughly into his routine that skipping it feels almost unthinkable. Before school begins, he jogs along the sandy shoreline, where gentle waves roll steadily onto the beach and a light breeze drifts in from the open sea, carrying with it the faint, unmistakable scent of salt that he has come to associate with calm concentration and quiet determination, and this disciplined early-morning practice has gradually transformed him, over the course of many months, into a runner possessing far greater stamina than he once had, a change that even his classmates have begun to notice and remark upon.

While he runs, Yousef engages in a private mental exercise that he has practiced since he was considerably younger, having discovered early on how much more enjoyable running could become through deliberate imagination: he likes to visualize himself racing against the wind itself, as though it were a playful, invisible rival jogging directly beside him stride for stride, matching his every movement with uncanny precision, pumping his arms rhythmically and accelerating his pace as the breeze rushes past his face, as if the wind itself were struggling to keep up. This small act of deliberate visualization transforms even the most grueling stretches of his run into something genuinely exhilarating rather than merely exhausting, and it has become an indispensable technique on which he relies whenever running begins to feel especially arduous.

When his school announces an upcoming cross-country race that the entire class has been anticipating eagerly throughout the year, a long, winding course that loops twice around the whole school field and tests not merely raw speed but genuine endurance and mental fortitude, every student is expected to participate and contribute their very best effort. Partway through the actual race, however, Yousef suddenly feels utterly exhausted, and doubt begins to creep steadily into his mind, whispering that he might as well ease off and accept a mediocre finish, while his chest burns sharply and his legs feel impossibly heavy beneath him.

Just then, he remembers his favorite morning game from the coast, the one ritual that has never once failed him in moments of difficulty, and he briefly closes his eyes, visualizing the wind racing beside him once again exactly as it does during his quiet mornings at home. Drawing on sheer perseverance, he forces his tired legs to move faster and faster, refusing to let the creeping doubt win, and before long his strength and confidence return in full force, almost as though the wind itself had generously lent him a portion of its boundless energy.

Yousef ultimately crosses the finish line with one final, determined burst of speed, his classmates cheering loudly from the sidelines as he passes them by, and although he does not finish in first place, he has poured every ounce of perseverance he possesses into the race from start to finish, holding absolutely nothing back for the final stretch. His coach claps enthusiastically and tells him how proud he is, not only of his effort, but also of the remarkable endurance and steady pace he maintained all the way to the finish line, a lesson in perseverance that Yousef will carry with him long after the race has ended and the cheering crowd has finally gone home.

versions.text:
For as long as he can remember, Yousef has loved running, and scarcely a single morning passes without a quiet run along the Red Sea coast near his home, a ritual that has become every bit as essential to his day as breakfast itself, woven so thoroughly into his routine that skipping it feels almost inconceivable to him. Before school begins each day, he jogs along the sandy shoreline, where gentle waves roll steadily onto the beach and a light breeze drifts in from the open sea, carrying with it the faint, unmistakable scent of salt that he has long since come to associate with calm concentration and quiet, resolute determination; this disciplined early-morning practice has gradually transformed him, over the course of many months, into a runner possessing considerably greater stamina than he once had, a transformation that even his classmates have begun to notice and remark upon with evident admiration.

While running, Yousef engages in a private mental exercise that he has practiced since he was considerably younger, having discovered early on how much more enjoyable running could become through deliberate, sustained imagination: he likes to visualize himself racing against the wind itself, as though it were a playful, invisible rival jogging directly beside him stride for stride, matching his every movement with uncanny, almost supernatural precision, pumping his arms rhythmically and steadily accelerating his pace as the breeze rushes past his face, as if the wind itself were straining to keep up with him. This small, deliberate act of visualization transforms even the most grueling stretches of his run into something genuinely exhilarating rather than merely exhausting, and it has become an utterly indispensable technique on which he consistently relies whenever running begins to feel especially arduous or discouraging.

When his school announces an upcoming cross-country race that the entire class has been anticipating eagerly throughout the year, a long, winding course that loops twice around the whole school field and tests not merely raw speed but genuine endurance and mental fortitude, every student is expected to participate and contribute their very best effort, regardless of natural athletic ability. Partway through the actual race, however, Yousef suddenly feels utterly exhausted, and doubt begins to creep steadily and insistently into his mind, whispering that he might as well ease off and quietly accept a mediocre, unremarkable finish, while his chest burns sharply and his legs feel impossibly heavy beneath him with every labored stride.

Just then, he remembers his favorite morning game from the coast, the one ritual that has never once failed him in moments of genuine difficulty, and he briefly closes his eyes, visualizing the wind racing beside him once again exactly as it does during his quiet mornings at home. Drawing on sheer perseverance, he forces his exhausted legs to move faster and faster still, resolutely refusing to let the creeping doubt prevail, and before long his strength and confidence return to him in full force, almost as though the wind itself had generously lent him some small portion of its boundless, restless energy.

Yousef ultimately crosses the finish line with one final, determined burst of speed, his classmates cheering loudly and enthusiastically from the sidelines as he passes them by, and although he does not finish in first place, he has poured every last ounce of perseverance he possesses into the race from start to finish, holding absolutely nothing back for the demanding final stretch. His coach claps enthusiastically and tells him how genuinely proud he is, not only of his effort, but also of the remarkable endurance and steady, controlled pace he maintained all the way to the finish line, a lesson in perseverance that Yousef will carry with him long after the race has ended and the cheering crowd has finally dispersed and gone home.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: A boy imagines racing the wind to finish a hard race.
Yousef is the fastest runner in his whole school.
Yousef's coach teaches him how to swim competitively.
The wind in the story literally helps Yousef run faster by pushing him forward.
questions.why: The story centers on how Yousef's imagined game with the wind helps him stay determined when he becomes exhausted during the race.

wrong.B: The story never claims Yousef is the fastest runner in his school.
wrong.C: Swimming is never mentioned; the story is about running.
wrong.D: The wind game is a mental trick, not something that really moves him faster.

questions.stem: Where does Yousef do his daily running practice?
options: At his school's running track
Along the coast near his home
In the stadium
At a sports park downtown
questions.why: The story says Yousef jogs along the coast near his home every morning.

wrong.A: The story does not mention a school running track for practice.
wrong.D: The story does not mention a downtown park.

questions.stem: What happens to Yousef partway through the actual race?
options: He trips and falls on the track
He decides to stop running completely
He feels exhausted and wants to slow down
He becomes completely lost somewhere on the course
questions.why: The story says that partway through the race, Yousef feels completely exhausted and a voice urges him to slow down.

wrong.A: The story does not mention Yousef tripping or falling.
wrong.B: Yousef feels like stopping, but he does not actually stop.
wrong.D: The story does not say Yousef gets lost.

questions.stem: In the story, the word pace means —
options: a kind of running shoe
the distance of the whole race
a short rest during a race
how fast someone is moving
questions.why: The story describes Yousef pushing his pace faster and faster, showing that pace means how fast he is moving.

wrong.A: Pace does not refer to shoes.
wrong.B: Pace is about speed, not the race's total distance.
wrong.C: Pace is not a rest break.

questions.stem: Why does picturing the wind as a rival help Yousef keep going?
options: It makes hard running feel exciting.
It makes the actual wind blow him forward
It makes the race distance shorter
It tells him exactly when the race will end
questions.why: The game transforms exhausting stretches of the run into something thrilling, which motivates Yousef to keep pushing.

wrong.B: Imagining a rival does not change how the real wind behaves.
wrong.C: The race stays the same length regardless of the game.
wrong.D: The game does not tell him when the race will end.

questions.stem: What does Yousef's reaction after finishing, even though he does not come in first, suggest about what matters most to him?
options: Beating every other runner no matter what
Giving his full effort and determination
Getting attention from his classmates
Running exactly like his coach
questions.why: Yousef feels proud of pouring his full determination into the race, even without finishing first, showing effort matters most to him.

wrong.A: He accepts not finishing first without being upset.
wrong.C: The story focuses on his effort, not on attention from others.
wrong.D: The story does not compare his running style to his coach's.

questions.stem: Why does Yousef's pace slow down in the middle of the race?
options: The coach tells him to slow down
The wind is blowing against him too strongly
His legs feel heavy and he becomes exhausted
Another runner pushes him off the path
questions.why: Yousef's legs feel impossibly heavy because he becomes exhausted, which causes him to want to slow down.

wrong.A: The coach does not tell him to slow down during the race.
wrong.B: The story does not say the real wind blocks his path.
wrong.D: No other runner pushes him in the story.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the events in this story?
options: By comparing Yousef's race to a race from long ago
By listing rules for cross-country races
By describing the race before explaining Yousef's daily practice
By describing his practice first, then the real race.
questions.why: The story first explains Yousef's coastal practice and his wind game, then shows how that game helps him during the actual race.

wrong.A: The story does not compare races from different time periods.
wrong.B: No rules for racing are listed.
wrong.C: The practice is described first, not after the race.

MID.prompt: Explain how Yousef's imagination game helps him deal with tiredness during the race. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how the game helps Yousef.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Yousef's imagination game helps him in two ways. First, it turns the hardest parts of running into something exciting instead of exhausting, because he pictures the wind as a playful rival. Second, when he becomes exhausted during the actual race, remembering the game gives him fresh determination, and he pushes his legs faster until his strength returns.

keyWords.definition: the quality of continuing to try hard at something difficult without giving up
keyWords.example: The climber's perseverance helped her reach the top of the mountain.

keyWords.definition: to form a clear picture of something in your mind
keyWords.example: Athletes often visualize their performance before a big competition.

keyWords.definition: the physical or mental energy needed to keep doing something difficult for a long time
extremely exciting and full of energy
keyWords.example: The roller coaster ride was absolutely exhilarating.

keyWords.definition: the ability to keep doing something difficult or painful for a long time
keyWords.example: Marathon runners train for months to build their endurance.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the story?
options: Yousef uses visualization to push past exhaustion and finish proudly.
Yousef's visualization technique literally changes the weather during the race.
Winning first place is the only way Yousef measures success.
The story mainly explains the history of cross-country racing.
questions.why: The story focuses on how Yousef's mental technique and perseverance help him overcome exhaustion and finish the race proudly, even without finishing first.

wrong.B: Visualization is a mental trick; it does not change real weather.
wrong.C: Yousef is proud of his effort, showing success means more than first place to him.
wrong.D: The story does not explain the history of the sport.

questions.stem: In the story, the word stamina most nearly means —
options: a short burst of speed
lasting energy to keep going
a kind of running shoe
the feeling of being afraid
questions.why: The story describes Yousef's practice giving him far greater stamina, meaning more lasting energy for running.

wrong.A: Stamina is about lasting energy, not a quick burst of speed.
wrong.C: Stamina is not a type of footwear.

questions.stem: According to the story, what specifically happens to Yousef partway through the race?
options: He collides with another runner
He stops to rest at a water station
He becomes exhausted and doubts himself
He realizes he is lost and turns around
questions.why: The story explicitly states that partway through the race Yousef becomes utterly exhausted and doubt begins to creep into his mind.

wrong.A: No collision with another runner is described.
wrong.B: The story does not mention a water station.
wrong.D: Yousef does not get lost in the story.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about why Yousef's visualization game works so well for him?
options: It physically makes the wind push him forward
It guarantees he will finish first
It removes all the pain from running
It renews his determination to keep going
questions.why: By imagining an exciting race against the wind, Yousef's attention shifts away from his exhaustion, which restores his determination to keep running.

wrong.A: Visualizing does not change how the actual wind behaves.
wrong.B: He still does not finish first, so it is not a guarantee of winning.
wrong.C: His chest still burns and his legs still feel heavy, so the pain is not removed.

questions.stem: What causes Yousef's strength and confidence to return during the race?
options: He visualizes racing the wind
The race route becomes shorter near the end
His coach runs alongside him
The wind physically slows down so he can rest
questions.why: The story shows that when Yousef visualizes racing the wind again and draws on perseverance, his strength and confidence return.

wrong.B: The race distance does not change partway through.
wrong.C: The coach is not described as running beside him during the race.
wrong.D: The actual wind does not slow down to help him.

questions.stem: Which list places these events in the correct order?
options: The race begins; Yousef becomes exhausted; Yousef starts his morning coastal practice
He begins his coastal practice, the race is announced, exhaustion hits, and he visualizes the wind to finish.
Yousef finishes the race; the school announces the race; Yousef begins practicing
Yousef becomes exhausted; the school announces the race; Yousef begins practicing
questions.why: Yousef's coastal practice and wind game come first, then the school announces the race, then he becomes exhausted during the race, and finally he visualizes the wind again and finishes.

wrong.A: His coastal practice begins long before the actual race, not after.
wrong.C: He cannot finish the race before it is even announced.
wrong.D: He cannot become exhausted in a race that has not yet been announced.

questions.stem: How is Yousef's effort during his morning practice similar to his effort during the actual cross-country race?
options: In both, he runs with a group of friends
In both, he comes in first place
In both, he visualizes to keep pushing
In both, he runs for exactly the same distance
questions.why: In his morning practice and in the race, Yousef relies on visualizing the wind and summoning determination to keep going.

wrong.A: The story does not describe him running with friends in either setting.
wrong.B: He does not finish first in the race, so this cannot be a shared similarity.
wrong.D: The story never states that both runs cover the exact same distance.

questions.stem: Why does the author most likely include the detail that Yousef does not finish first, yet his coach is still proud?
options: To suggest that coaches are never satisfied with their runners
To show that winning does not require any effort
To prove that cross-country races are not competitive
To show that effort matters more than finishing first
questions.why: By showing the coach's pride despite Yousef not finishing first, the author highlights that genuine effort and perseverance are what truly matter.

wrong.A: The coach's pride shows the opposite: he is satisfied with Yousef's effort.
wrong.B: The story shows that effort, not the absence of it, leads to pride.
wrong.C: The race clearly has competitors and a finishing order, so it is competitive.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says imagining a fun game while you practice makes hard work feel easier. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about Yousef's practice and his race.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that imagining a fun game while practicing makes hard work feel easier. Yousef's habit of visualizing himself racing the wind turns his difficult coastal practice into something exhilarating rather than exhausting, and that same mental game gives him the perseverance he needs when he becomes utterly exhausted during the real race. Someone might argue that imagination cannot actually change how tired your body feels, but Yousef's steady pace and strong finish suggest that shifting your focus really can help you push through real physical exhaustion.
